questions.q: What was the immediate trigger that led Maharaja Hari Singh to sign the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947?
questions.a: The immediate trigger was the invasion of Kashmir by Pakistani tribal militias (supported by the Pakistani army) on 22 October 1947, which threatened Srinagar. A wrong answer (e.g., "the Maharaja voluntarily wanted to join India" or "pressure from Sheikh Abdullah") reveals a misunderstanding of the coercive circumstances and the role of external aggression in forcing the accession.

questions.q: Why did India accept a conditional accession for J&K (with reference to a plebiscite and internal autonomy) while integrating other princely states unconditionally?
questions.a: India accepted conditionality because: (a) the accession occurred under military emergency, (b) Prime Minister Nehru promised a plebiscite once law and order was restored (to demonstrate democratic credentials internationally), and (c) the Muslim-majority character of the state required political accommodation with the popular leader Sheikh Abdullah. A wrong answer (e.g., "because J&K was larger" or "because of Article 370") confuses cause and effect — Article 370 was the constitutional manifestation of the conditional accession, not its cause.

questions.q: A student argues: "Article 370 was a permanent provision that could not be amended without the concurrence of the J&K Constituent Assembly, which dissolved in 1957, so it became immutable." Identify the constitutional flaw in this argument.
questions.a: The flaw: Article 370(3) allowed the President to declare it inoperative or modify it *with the recommendation of the J&K Constituent Assembly*. After the Assembly dissolved, the Supreme Court (in *Sampat Prakash*, 1969) held that the President could still act with the concurrence of the *state government* (which meant the Governor's administration under President's Rule). The 2019 abrogation used this route. A wrong answer shows ignorance of the distinction between "Constituent Assembly" and "State Government" in the presidential orders.

questions.q: Compare the constitutional pathways used to integrate Hyderabad (1948) and J&K (1947–1954). Which pathway created a stronger legal foundation for central authority, and why?
questions.a: Hyderabad: military action → Standstill Agreement ended → full integration via merger agreement (1949) → regular state under Constitution. J&K: conditional accession → Article 370 → series of presidential orders extending Union powers. Hyderabad's pathway created a stronger *immediate* legal foundation because it resulted in unconditional merger before the Constitution came into force. J&K's pathway created a *negotiated* foundation that required continuous political management. A wrong answer that claims "Article 370 made integration stronger" confuses autonomy with integration.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The Shimla Agreement (1972) made the UN resolutions on Kashmir obsolete by converting the ceasefire line into the Line of Control and mandating bilateral resolution."
questions.a: The statement is partially correct but incomplete. The Shimla Agreement did establish the LoC and commit both sides to bilateral talks, *but* it did not formally annul UN Security Council Resolutions 47 (1948) and 91 (1951), which remain on the UN agenda. Pakistan continues to invoke them; India argues they are superseded by Shimla and later by the Lahore Declaration (1999). A wrong answer that says "UN resolutions are completely dead" ignores their continued diplomatic utility for Pakistan.

questions.q: Draft a one-paragraph constitutional argument *either* supporting *or* opposing the 2019 abrogation of Article 370, using only the text of Article 370(3) and the 1954 Presidential Order (CO 272).
questions.a: A good answer will cite: Article 370(3) requires "recommendation of the Constituent Assembly" for abrogation; the 1954 Order (CO 272) replaced "Constituent Assembly" with "Legislative Assembly" via Article 367 interpretation. The argument must address whether a Governor's administration under President's Rule can substitute for an elected assembly. A poor answer merely repeats political slogans ("integral part" or "betrayal") without engaging the constitutional text.
